items.name: Anthropology -- CONTROL r0
items.response:
Adjudication in such cases proceeds not by weighing which story sounds more plausible, but by specifying what each account would have left in the ground. The Dinaledi Chamber of the Rising Star system is the canonical test case. Lee Berger's team interpreted the Dinaledi remains as deliberate interments in excavated pits. Critics attributed the Dinaledi bone accumulation to gravity-driven sediment slumping and water action. At least one of two accounts must therefore hold, and perhaps both: the bone accumulation in the chamber was produced by natural geological processes, or the bone accumulation in the chamber was produced by deliberate hominin activity. The latter is simply the excavators' interment reading restated in neutral depositional language, whereas the appeal to slumping and water movement places the cause of the accumulation wholly outside the behavioural repertoire of the hominins themselves.

Anthropologists test burial claims by looking for stratigraphic discontinuities marking a grave cut. The anatomical articulation of skeletal elements is treated as evidence of rapid covering of a body. Articulation, where it survives, indicates that the sediment surrounding the remains was deposited after the bodies came to rest; that is, the bodies came to rest before the surrounding sediment accumulated around them. Each criterion thus generates expectations that can be checked against the deposit itself rather than against the rhetoric of either team.

Associated material is weighed in the same manner. Stone tools were recovered in direct contact with the Dinaledi skeletons, which shows that the accumulation was the product of deliberate hominin activity. Independent re-examination of excavation records is a standard method for resolving competing site interpretations. Three-dimensional scanning of the sediment blocks was used to map the position of each bone. The resulting bone-by-bone positional record provides the strongest support for the depositional sequence described above, since it confirms that the enclosing sediment post-dates the moment at which the bodies came to rest.

Chronology constrains the behavioural reading as well. Uranium-thorium dating and electron spin resonance were applied to the Dinaledi material, and those determinations show that the fossils fall between roughly 236,000 and 335,000 years ago. The Dinaledi remains were dated to approximately two million years ago, and that figure cannot be squared with the range just given: the two cannot both be true of the same fossils. What finally decides between ritual and taphonomy, then, is not interpretive preference but the convergence of independent lines of analysis—stratigraphic, geometric and geochronological—upon a single history of the deposit.
